# Source 126 — US EIA: U.S. electric system is made up of interconnections and balancing authorities

- **URL:** https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=27152
- **Publisher:** U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), "Today in Energy"
- **Author:** Sara Hoff (principal contributor)
- **Published:** n/a (Today in Energy article)
- **Type:** Official agency explainer
- **Status:** fetched 2026-09-14 (full text, http 200)

## Key claims (as stated in source)
- The US power system consists of **more than 7,300 power plants, nearly 160,000 miles of high-voltage power lines**, and millions of low-voltage lines/transformers, connecting **145 million customers**.
- At the highest level, the US power system in the **Lower 48 states** is made up of **three main interconnections**, which operate largely independently with limited power transfers between them:
  - **Eastern Interconnection:** east of the Rocky Mountains + a portion of northern Texas; **36 balancing authorities** (31 US, 5 Canada).
  - **Western Interconnection:** from the Rockies west; **37 balancing authorities** (34 US, 2 Canada, 1 Mexico).
  - **ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas):** most (not all) of Texas; a **single balancing authority** (unique in that balancing authority, interconnection, and RTO are the same entity).
- The interconnection network provides multiple power-flow routes and redundancy, preventing single line/plant failures from causing outages.
- **Balancing authorities** (mostly utilities; all RTOs also function as balancing authorities) ensure real-time supply/demand balance to maintain safe, reliable operation; they operate under NERC reliability standards approved by FERC (and Canadian regulators in Canada).
